# Time Series

Each stock's own history, one stock at a time. `period` counts rows of the data (trading days), not calendar days.

## Window rules

Every rolling operator follows one of three rules for how much history it needs and what a missing day does. The toy
data shows all three on **C**, which has no price on Jan 04.

| Rule | Operators | A value once the window holds | A missing day in the window |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Part of the window** | `ts_mean`, `ts_std`, `ts_sum`, `ts_max`, `ts_min`, `ts_var`, `ts_quantile`, the pair operators, `volatility`, `volume`, `adv` | `min(20, period)` values | is skipped, as long as enough values remain |
| **The whole window** | `ts_rank`, `ts_argmax`, `ts_argmin`, `ts_skew`, `ts_kurt`, `decay_linear` | `period` values | hides the result until it has left the window |
| **Exponential** | `ewma`, `ewma_var`, `ewma_cov`, `ts_beta_ewma` | one value | is skipped; the average carries on |

With a window of 20 days or less, part of the window needs every day too, as in the 3-day panels below. The difference
shows on longer windows: a 60-day mean needs 20 values and skips the gaps between them.
[How qex Evaluates](../concepts.md#windows-and-history) explains why each rule is what it is.

## Rolling statistics

### ts_mean

<p class="sig"><code>ts_mean(x, period)</code></p>

The mean of each stock's last `period` values. Part of the window.

`close()`

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan 02 | 10.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 40.0 |
| Jan 03 | 11.0 | 19.0 | 30.5 | 42.0 |
| Jan 04 | 12.0 | 18.0 | · | 41.0 |
| Jan 05 | 11.0 | 18.5 | 31.0 | 43.0 |
| Jan 08 | 13.0 | 17.0 | 32.0 | 44.0 |
| Jan 09 | 14.0 | 16.0 | 31.5 | 46.0 |

Result: `ts_mean(close(), 3)`

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan 02 | · | · | · | · |
| Jan 03 | · | · | · | · |
| Jan 04 | 11.00 | 19.00 | · | 41.00 |
| Jan 05 | 11.33 | 18.50 | · | 42.00 |
| Jan 08 | 12.00 | 17.83 | · | 42.67 |
| Jan 09 | 12.67 | 17.17 | 31.50 | 44.33 |

```qex
ts_mean(returns(1), 20)                    # average daily return over a month
close() / ts_mean(close(), 200) - 1        # distance from the 200-day average
```

### ts_std

<p class="sig"><code>ts_std(x, period)</code></p>

The standard deviation of the window (sample, n − 1). Part of the window.

```qex
ts_std(returns(1), 20)                     # daily volatility, not annualized
```

### ts_var

<p class="sig"><code>ts_var(x, period)</code></p>

The variance of the window, `ts_std` squared. Part of the window.

### ts_sum

<p class="sig"><code>ts_sum(x, period)</code></p>

The sum of the window. Part of the window.

```qex
ts_sum(log(1 + returns(1)), 20)            # the 20-day log return, from daily returns
```

<p class="sig"><code>ts_max(x, period)</code></p>

The largest value in the window. Part of the window.

```qex
close() / ts_max(close(), 252)             # how far below the 52-week high
```

### ts_min

<p class="sig"><code>ts_min(x, period)</code></p>

The smallest value in the window. Part of the window.

### ts_quantile

<p class="sig"><code>ts_quantile(x, period, q[, min_periods])</code></p>

The `q`-quantile of the window, `q` from 0 to 1, interpolating between the two nearest values: 0.5 is the median, 0
and 1 are `ts_min` and `ts_max`. Part of the window; `min_periods` changes the minimum.

```qex
-ts_quantile(returns(1), 252, 0.05)                                     # 5% value-at-risk, as a loss
ts_quantile(returns(1), 60, 0.75) - ts_quantile(returns(1), 60, 0.25)   # interquartile range
```

## Lag and difference

### delay

<p class="sig"><code>delay(x, period)</code></p>

The value `period` rows ago; `period` ≥ 0. There is no negative delay: a value can only come from the past.

`close()`

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan 02 | 10.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 40.0 |
| Jan 03 | 11.0 | 19.0 | 30.5 | 42.0 |
| Jan 04 | 12.0 | 18.0 | · | 41.0 |
| Jan 05 | 11.0 | 18.5 | 31.0 | 43.0 |
| Jan 08 | 13.0 | 17.0 | 32.0 | 44.0 |
| Jan 09 | 14.0 | 16.0 | 31.5 | 46.0 |

Result: `delay(close(), 1)`

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan 02 | · | · | · | · |
| Jan 03 | 10.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 40.0 |
| Jan 04 | 11.0 | 19.0 | 30.5 | 42.0 |
| Jan 05 | 12.0 | 18.0 | · | 41.0 |
| Jan 08 | 11.0 | 18.5 | 31.0 | 43.0 |
| Jan 09 | 13.0 | 17.0 | 32.0 | 44.0 |

```qex
delay(returns(231), 21)                    # 12-month momentum, skipping the last month
```

### delta

<p class="sig"><code>delta(x, period)</code></p>

Today's value minus the value `period` rows ago: `x - delay(x, period)`. Missing when either is.

```qex
delta(returns(20), 5)                      # how momentum changed over a week
```

## Ranking and extremes

### ts_rank

<p class="sig"><code>ts_rank(x, period)</code></p>

Where today's value ranks among the stock's last `period` values, from `1/period` (the lowest) to `1` (the highest);

## Pairs of series

> **Regressions through time, one stock at a time**
>
> The pair operators work down **each stock's own history**: `ts_beta(y, x, 252)` fits one regression per stock, on
> that stock's last 252 days, so every stock gets its own beta, alpha and residual. `x` is usually one series for
> every stock, such as the market's return. For a regression **across the stocks on one day**, use
> [`regression_neut`](cross-sectional.md#regression_neut);
> [Two kinds of regression](../concepts.md#two-kinds-of-regression) sets them side by side.

The pair operators use only the days on which both series have a value. `min_periods` (default `min(20, period)`) is
the fewest such days a window needs: with the default, a stock 20 days after listing gets a "252-day" beta from 20
days. Ask for more when it matters.

### ts_corr

<p class="sig"><code>ts_corr(x, y, period[, min_periods])</code></p>

The correlation of `x` and `y` over the window. Part of the window. Over the window's $n$ paired days,

$$
\rho_{xy} = \frac{\sum_t (x_t - \bar x)(y_t - \bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum_t (x_t - \bar x)^2 \, \sum_t (y_t - \bar y)^2}}
$$

```qex
ts_corr(abs(returns(1)), volume(1), 60)    # do big moves come with volume?
```

### ts_cov

<p class="sig"><code>ts_cov(x, y, period[, min_periods])</code></p>

The covariance of `x` and `y` over the window. Part of the window.

$$
\mathrm{cov}(x, y) = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_t (x_t - \bar x)(y_t - \bar y)
$$

### ts_beta

<p class="sig"><code>ts_beta(y, x, period[, min_periods])</code></p>

The least-squares slope of `y` on `x` over the window: the $\beta$ of $y_t = \alpha + \beta x_t + \varepsilon_t$, fitted
on the paired days. Part of the window.

$$
\beta = \frac{\mathrm{cov}(y, x)}{\mathrm{var}(x)} = \frac{\sum_t (x_t - \bar x)(y_t - \bar y)}{\sum_t (x_t - \bar x)^2}
$$

```qex
ts_beta(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 252)          # market beta
ts_beta(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 252, 126)     # no value until 126 days are paired
```

### ts_beta_shrunk

<p class="sig"><code>ts_beta_shrunk(y, x, period[, min_periods][, groups])</code></p>

`ts_beta`, pulled toward the day's average beta in proportion to its own noise (Vasicek 1973). For stock $i$, with
$\beta_i$ its `ts_beta` from $n_i$ paired days:

$$
\beta_i^{\text{shrunk}} = w_i \, \beta_i + (1 - w_i) \, \bar\beta,
\qquad
w_i = \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + s_i^2}
$$

- $\bar\beta$ and $\tau^2$ are the mean and variance of the day's betas across the stocks in the universe: the prior.
- $s_i^2$ is the sampling variance of stock $i$'s own estimate, from its residual variance $\hat\sigma_i^2$:

$$
s_i^2 = \frac{\hat\sigma_i^2}{(n_i - 1)\mathrm{var}(x)},
\qquad
\hat\sigma_i^2 = \frac{n_i - 1}{n_i - 2}\left(\mathrm{var}(y_i) - \beta_i^2 \mathrm{var}(x)\right)
$$

This is the posterior mean of $\beta_i$ under a normal prior $N(\bar\beta, \tau^2)$. A precise estimate ($s_i^2$ small
against $\tau^2$) keeps its own beta; a beta from a short or noisy history moves most of the way to the average.
[Market Beta](https://marketneutral.github.io/alpha-parser/examples/market-beta/#shrinking-beta) discusses when it helps.

**A prior for each group.** With `groups` (a group's name or any labels expression), $\bar\beta$ and $\tau^2$ are the
mean and variance of the betas in the stock's own group that day: a utility's beta is pulled toward the utilities',
not toward the market's average. A stock with no group has no value. A group with fewer than two betas that day has
no spread to shrink by, so its stocks keep their own betas.

How qex tells the two optional arguments apart: a number written as a number is `min_periods`, and anything else
(a quoted name, a labels expression) is `groups`. So `groups` comes last, after `min_periods` when there is one, and
`min_periods` is written out (`126`, not `252 / 2`); qex refuses either mistake with a message that says which.

```qex
ts_beta_shrunk(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 252)                  # toward the day's average beta
ts_beta_shrunk(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 252, 'sector')        # toward each sector's
ts_beta_shrunk(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 252, 126, 'sector')   # and a value only from 126 paired days
```

### ts_alpha

<p class="sig"><code>ts_alpha(y, x1, ..., xk, period[, min_periods])</code></p>

The intercept of the same regression: the $\alpha$ of $y_t = \alpha + \beta x_t + \varepsilon_t$ over the window. A
least-squares line goes through the two means, so over the window's paired days

$$
\alpha = \bar y - \beta \, \bar x
$$

Both means are over the days both series have a value, the same days as the beta. (Writing it by hand with two
`ts_mean`s gets this wrong whenever `y` has a gap in the window that `x` doesn't.) Part of the window, with
`ts_beta`'s minimum. For a stock's daily return on the market's it is the daily alpha, Jensen's alpha without the
risk-free rate; times 252 for a year.

```qex
ts_alpha(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 252) * 252     # annualized
```

**Several regressors.** Give more than one `x` and it is one joint least-squares fit over the window's days where `y`
and every `x` have a value:

$$
y_t = \alpha + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j \, x_{j,t} + \varepsilon_t
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\alpha = \bar y - \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j \, \bar x_j
$$

with the $\beta_j$ solving the window's normal equations, $\mathrm{cov}(x, x)\,\beta = \mathrm{cov}(x, y)$.
The alpha is net of all the regressors at once, which is not the same as taking them out one at a time when they are
correlated. A window needs at least $k + 2$ such days (and `min_periods`); regressors that duplicate each other get
the minimum-norm fit. A multi-factor alpha, with factor returns supplied once per day for every stock
([Data Format](https://marketneutral.github.io/alpha-parser/data/format/#date-only-fields-and-the-market)):

```qex
ts_alpha(returns(1), field('mkt'), field('smb'), field('hml'), 252) * 252
```

The shrunk versions take one regressor: shrinking several betas at once needs a prior across them, which is a model
of its own.

### ts_alpha_shrunk

<p class="sig"><code>ts_alpha_shrunk(y, x, period[, min_periods][, groups])</code></p>

The intercept that goes with `ts_beta_shrunk`'s slope. For a fixed slope, the least-squares intercept is still the
line through the means:

$$
\alpha^{\text{shrunk}} = \bar y - \beta^{\text{shrunk}} \, \bar x
$$

It differs from `ts_alpha` by exactly what the shrinkage took off the beta, times the average of `x`:

$$
\alpha^{\text{shrunk}} - \alpha = (\beta - \beta^{\text{shrunk}}) \, \bar x
$$

In a rising market, a low beta shrunk up toward the average lowers the stock's alpha: part of what looked like alpha
was low beta. `groups` is as in `ts_beta_shrunk`.

```qex
ts_alpha_shrunk(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 252, 'sector') * 252
```

### ts_resid

<p class="sig"><code>ts_resid(y, x1, ..., xk, period[, min_periods])</code></p>

Today's residual from the window's fit, with $\alpha$ and the $\beta_j$ from the window ending today:

$$
\varepsilon_t = y_t - \alpha - \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j \, x_{j,t}
$$

The part of today's `y` that `x` doesn't explain: for a stock's return on the market's, its idiosyncratic return. No
value on a day `y` or `x` is missing. The fit includes today, as any rolling regression's last residual does; it
uses nothing after today.

```qex
ts_sum(ts_resid(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 252), 20)         # last month, beyond beta
ts_resid(returns(1), field('mkt'), field('smb'), field('hml'), 252)    # beyond three factors
```

### ts_resid_shrunk

<p class="sig"><code>ts_resid_shrunk(y, x, period[, min_periods][, groups])</code></p>

Today's residual from `ts_beta_shrunk`'s fit: $y_t - \alpha^{\text{shrunk}} - \beta^{\text{shrunk}} x_t$. `groups` is
as in `ts_beta_shrunk`.

```qex
-ts_sum(ts_resid_shrunk(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 252, 'sector'), 5)   # idiosyncratic reversal
```

## Exponentially weighted

A day's weight halves every `halflife` days, so the effective look-back is about three half-lives. There is no warm-up:
a value from the first observation, carried through missing days. With half-life $h$, a value $k$ days old has weight

$$
w_k = 2^{-k/h}
$$

### ewma

<p class="sig"><code>ewma(x, halflife)</code></p>

The exponentially weighted mean, over the days $x$ has a value:

$$
m_t = \frac{\sum_{k \ge 0} w_k \, x_{t-k}}{\sum_{k \ge 0} w_k}
$$

Below, **C** keeps its average through Jan 04.

`close()`

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan 02 | 10.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 40.0 |
| Jan 03 | 11.0 | 19.0 | 30.5 | 42.0 |
| Jan 04 | 12.0 | 18.0 | · | 41.0 |
| Jan 05 | 11.0 | 18.5 | 31.0 | 43.0 |
| Jan 08 | 13.0 | 17.0 | 32.0 | 44.0 |
| Jan 09 | 14.0 | 16.0 | 31.5 | 46.0 |

Result: `ewma(close(), 2)`

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan 02 | 10.00 | 20.00 | 30.00 | 40.00 |
| Jan 03 | 10.59 | 19.41 | 30.29 | 41.17 |
| Jan 04 | 11.23 | 18.77 | 30.29 | 41.09 |
| Jan 05 | 11.14 | 18.67 | 30.67 | 41.84 |
| Jan 08 | 11.80 | 18.07 | 31.25 | 42.61 |
| Jan 09 | 12.54 | 17.38 | 31.34 | 43.74 |

```qex
ewma(returns(1), 10)                       # a 10-day half-life average return
```

### ewma_var

<p class="sig"><code>ewma_var(x, halflife)</code></p>

The exponentially weighted variance.

```qex
sqrt(ewma_var(returns(1), 20) * 252)       # an annualized volatility that adapts quickly
```

### ewma_cov

<p class="sig"><code>ewma_cov(x, y, halflife)</code></p>

The exponentially weighted covariance, over the days both have a value.

### ts_beta_ewma

<p class="sig"><code>ts_beta_ewma(y, x, halflife)</code></p>

The exponentially weighted version of `ts_beta`, over the days both have a value:

$$
\beta_t = \frac{\mathrm{cov}_h(y, x)}{\mathrm{var}_h(x)}
$$

```qex
ts_beta_ewma(returns(1), returns(1, 'market'), 63)     # a beta that adapts within a quarter
```

## Shape of the window

### decay_linear

<p class="sig"><code>decay_linear(x, period)</code></p>

A weighted mean with weights `period`, `period − 1`, …, 1, the newest heaviest. The whole window. With period $p$:

$$
\text{decay}_t = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} (p - k)\, x_{t-k}}{p(p+1)/2}
$$

On Jan 04, **A** is (3 × 12 + 2 × 11 + 1 × 10) / 6.

`close()`

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan 02 | 10.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 | 40.0 |
| Jan 03 | 11.0 | 19.0 | 30.5 | 42.0 |
| Jan 04 | 12.0 | 18.0 | · | 41.0 |
| Jan 05 | 11.0 | 18.5 | 31.0 | 43.0 |
| Jan 08 | 13.0 | 17.0 | 32.0 | 44.0 |
| Jan 09 | 14.0 | 16.0 | 31.5 | 46.0 |

Result: `decay_linear(close(), 3)`

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan 02 | · | · | · | · |
| Jan 03 | · | · | · | · |
| Jan 04 | 11.33 | 18.67 | · | 41.17 |
| Jan 05 | 11.33 | 18.42 | · | 42.17 |
| Jan 08 | 12.17 | 17.67 | · | 43.17 |
| Jan 09 | 13.17 | 16.75 | 31.58 | 44.83 |

```qex
decay_linear(returns(1), 10)               # a recency-weighted 10-day average
```

### ts_skew

<p class="sig"><code>ts_skew(x, period)</code></p>

The skewness of the window. The whole window.

```qex
-ts_skew(returns(1), 60)                   # prefer stocks without lottery-like upside
```

### ts_kurt

<p class="sig"><code>ts_kurt(x, period)</code></p>

The excess kurtosis of the window (0 for a normal distribution). The whole window.
